raw_text:
### Bioresorbable Vascular Scaffolds in Percutaneous Coronary Intervention: A Narrative Review

#### Introduction
The treatment of coronary artery disease (CAD) via percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) has evolved through successive paradigms, from plain old balloon angioplasty to bare-metal stents (BMS) and contemporary drug-eluting stents (DES). While contemporary metallic DES have minimized restenosis, they introduce permanent metallic cages that hinder vasomotion, trigger chronic local inflammatory reactions, and preclude future surgical bypass options [1, 2]. Bioresorbable vascular scaffolds (BVS) emerged as the "fourth revolution" in interventional cardiology [2], conceptualized to provide transient vessel patency and local drug release during the critical healing phase, followed by complete bioresorption to facilitate vascular restoration [1, 3].

#### The First-Generation Polymeric Platforms: Clinical Triumph and Setbacks
The first-generation Absorb BVS (Abbott Vascular), composed of a poly-L-lactic acid (PLLA) backbone with an everolimus-eluting poly-D,L-lactic acid coating, was initially validated in prospective studies such as the ABSORB Cohort A [1] and Cohort B [3] trials. These feasibility trials demonstrated successful acute mechanical performance, progressive vascular restoration, and late lumen enlargement upon complete polymer resorption. 

These promising findings led to large randomized controlled trials (RCTs). The ABSORB II trial was the first to compare BVS with cobalt-chromium everolimus-eluting stents (CoCr-EES), demonstrating similar clinical safety at one year [4]. However, the subsequent pivotal ABSORB III trial [5] and the real-world Amsterdam Investigator-Initiated Absorb Strategy All-Comers (AIDA) trial [6] raised serious concerns. Although early pooled patient-level meta-analyses suggested non-inferiority [7], 2-year outcomes showed an increased risk of target lesion failure (TLF) and scaffold thrombosis (ScT) with BVS [8].

At one year, the ABSORB IV trial reported higher rates of target vessel myocardial infarction (TV-MI) and target lesion revascularization (TLR) [9]. Over 5 years of follow-up in the ABSORB III trial [10] and pooled patient-level analyses [11], BVS was associated with significantly higher cumulative rates of TV-MI and scaffold thrombosis. Although this excess risk resolved after complete resorption at 3 years, the early clinical hazard prompted the market withdrawal of the first-generation Absorb BVS [10, 11].

#### Pathophysiology and the Importance of Implantation Technique
The failures of early-generation BVS prompted intensive research into their underlying mechanisms. Pathological and clinical studies identified several material and procedural factors. First, the mechanical properties of PLLA required thick struts (~150 µm) to achieve radial strength comparable to metallic DES (~60–80 µm) [12, 13]. These thick struts disrupted laminar blood flow, induced endothelial shear stress, and delayed endothelialization, thereby predisposing the treated segment to thrombosis [12, 13].

Intravascular imaging with optical coherence tomography (OCT) elucidated specific mechanical failure modes, including scaffold underexpansion, malapposition, late strut discontinuity, and neoatherosclerosis [14, 15]. Furthermore, early BVS use suffered from a lack of standardized implantation techniques, often deployed in small vessels (<2.25 mm) where thick struts easily occluded the lumen [16].

To address these limitations, experts developed the "PSP" (Pre-dilatation, Sizing, Post-dilatation) implantation protocol to optimize scaffold expansion and apposition [17, 18]. Real-world registries, such as GHOST-EU, confirmed that strict adherence to the PSP protocol significantly reduced the incidence of ScT and adverse cardiac events [17]. In response, the European Society of Cardiology (ESC) and the European Association of Percutaneous Cardiovascular Interventions (EAPCI) Task Force recommended restricting first-generation BVS to clinical trials and mandated strict PSP compliance combined with intravascular imaging guidance [19].

#### Next-Generation Bioresorbable Scaffolds: Polymeric and Metallic Innovations
The lessons from the first-generation polymer-based scaffolds catalyzed the development of refined next-generation platforms designed with thinner struts, superior polymers, or bioresorbable metals.

##### Metallic Magnesium Scaffolds
Bioresorbable metals, particularly magnesium, offer high radial strength and shorter resorption times. The PROGRESS-AMS trial first proved the feasibility of bare magnesium-alloy stents [20]. To control degradation and drug delivery, the BIOSOLVE-I trial evaluated a paclitaxel-eluting version [21]. The second-generation sirolimus-eluting resorbable magnesium scaffold (Magmaris, Biotronik) demonstrated excellent safety in the BIOSOLVE-II trial [22] and showed lower acute thrombogenicity than PLLA in ex vivo porcine models [23]. Long-term safety was confirmed in the BIOSOLVE-IV registry under real-world conditions [24]. The third-generation resorbable magnesium scaffold (DREAMS 3G), evaluated in the BIOMAG-I trial, features further strut thickness reduction and improved radial strength, showing low late lumen loss and minimal device thrombosis [25].

##### Thinner-Strut Polymeric Scaffolds
Several polymer-based next-generation scaffolds have also emerged. The Fantom scaffold (REVA Medical), constructed from a tyrosine-derived polycarbonate (Tyrocore), features thinner struts and full radiopacity, showing high safety in the FANTOM II trial [26]. The MeRes100 scaffold (Meril Life Sciences) uses ultra-thin (100 µm) PLLA struts, demonstrating zero scaffold thrombosis and favorable clinical outcomes in the MeRes-1 [27] and MeRes-1 Extend trials [28]. Similarly, the thin-strut (100–125 µm) sirolimus-eluting Firesorb BRS (MicroPort) showed excellent 1-year efficacy and zero device thrombosis in the FUTURE-III pooled analysis [29]. Lastly, iron-based bioresorbable scaffolds with ultra-thin metallic struts (IBS, Biotyx Medical) represent another frontier, showing highly promising clinical results in the IBS-FIM trial [30].

#### Conclusion
Bioresorbable vascular scaffolds continue to represent a highly appealing paradigm of "leave nothing behind" in PCI. While the first-generation PLLA scaffolds suffered from mechanical limitations and suboptimal implantation techniques, the integration of optimized deployment protocols and the advent of thinner-strut polymeric and magnesium-based metallic scaffolds have significantly improved safety and efficacy. Future clinical studies will determine if these next-generation technologies can permanently replace metallic stents in select patient subsets.
